reasoning: The proposal's core contribution—measuring how much better a (weak) model is at verifying a candidate answer than generating one, and whether this generate-vs-verify gap holds across task types—is a formalized, actively-studied quantity. "Mind the Gap" (ICLR 2025, arXiv 2412.02674) defines the generation-verification gap (GV-Gap) as the precision of a model's verification over its generations, measures it across tasks (GSM8K, MATH, QA), and shows it scales with model size; "Variation in Verification" (arXiv 2509.17995) runs controlled experiments varying verifier generation capability and difficulty, finding verifier generation capability correlates with verification performance and that smaller models verify worse. Multiple sources already report the proposal's headline empirical finding directly—that "accurate verification can almost be as hard as generation, especially with smaller models being worse at verification," and the factual GV-gap is traced in arXiv 2605.27564. The specific framing (one fixed small open-weight "weak overseer," exactly four task types adding code/summarization, reporting verify-minus-generate accuracy with CIs for scalable oversight) is a modest novel packaging, but the load-bearing problem and most of the contribution are covered by published work; remaining gaps (code + reference-summarization in the same sweep, the explicit weak-overseer scalable-oversight lens) are minor.

evidence.title: Mind the Gap: Examining the Self-Improvement Capabilities of Large Language Models (ICLR 2025)
evidence.summary: Defines the generation-verification gap (GV-Gap, absolute and relative) as the metric measuring how well a model verifies its own generations. Measures it across tasks (GSM8K, MATH, QA) and finds a variant scales monotonically with pretraining FLOPs (larger models -> larger gap), directly addressing the proposal's question of how much better verification is than generation and how it varies.

evidence.title: Variation in Verification: Understanding Verification Dynamics in Large Language Models
evidence.summary: Controlled experiments varying problem difficulty and verifier generation capability across reasoning domains. Finds verifier generation capability correlates with verification performance and that the verify-vs-generate relationship is difficulty-dependent (saturated/linear/threshold), directly addressing whether and how the generate-vs-verify gap holds for weaker models.

evidence.title: Verification Is Not Easier Than Generation In General
evidence.summary: Community post explicitly interrogating the load-bearing scalable-oversight assumption that verification is easier than generation, the exact premise the proposal aims to measure, noting it does not hold in general.

evidence.title: The Future of Facts: Tracing the Factual Generation-Verification Gap
evidence.summary: Studies the factual generation-verification gap, finding verification is learned before generation and is more robust, and that verifying whether an answer is correct is easier than generating one — covering the factual-QA slice of the proposed task-type sweep.

evidence.title: On scalable oversight with weak LLMs judging strong LLMs (NeurIPS 2024, Kenton et al.)
evidence.summary: Large-scale empirical study (9 tasks, ~5M model calls) of weak LLM judges evaluating stronger ones, directly testing whether the verification-easier-than-generation assumption underlying scalable oversight holds for weak overseers across task types.

evidence.title: When Does Verification Pay Off? A Closer Look at LLMs as Solution Verifiers
evidence.summary: Examines LLMs as solution verifiers and when verification accuracy exceeds generation, relevant to the proposal's verify-minus-generate accuracy comparison across difficulty/task settings.
